lessons.plainEnglish: In West Virginia everybody in a passenger vehicle wears a belt, and the driver — not each passenger — is the one held responsible for it. There is exactly one exception: an adult of 18 or over sitting in the back. Everyone else, front or back, adult or child, must be buckled. Children under 8 need a proper child safety seat rather than just a belt, unless they have already reached 4 feet 9 inches, at which point a normal belt fits them correctly and is enough.
lessons.whyItMatters: The handbook puts a number on it: belts cut the chance of injury or death in a collision by 45 to 50 percent. They work by spreading crash forces across the strongest parts of the body and keeping you from being thrown forward or out of the vehicle. A belt worn wrongly — lap belt up on the soft stomach instead of low across the hips — gives away much of that protection.
lessons.example: You are driving two friends. One is 19 and sits in the back; the other is 17 and sits in front. Legally the 19-year-old in the back is the single permitted exception, but the 17-year-old must be belted — and if they are not, it is you the driver who is responsible.

questions.question: Who must wear a safety belt in a passenger vehicle in West Virginia?
choices: Everyone in the vehicle, apart from one narrow exception
Only the driver
Only the driver and front-seat passenger
Only occupants under 18
questions.explanation: The handbook states that everyone in a passenger vehicle must wear a federally approved safety belt. The single legal exception is a person 18 or older riding in the back seat; a medical exception may also be issued with proof.

questions.question: Your front-seat passenger refuses to buckle up, saying it is their own choice. What does West Virginia law require?
choices: They must wear a belt — everyone in a passenger vehicle must be belted
It is their decision as an adult
Only passengers under 18 are required to buckle
Belts are required only on interstate highways
questions.explanation: Everyone in a passenger vehicle must wear a federally approved safety belt. A front-seat passenger is not covered by the back-seat exception, and the driver is responsible for ensuring passengers are buckled.

Each passenger individually
The vehicle's registered owner
The front-seat passenger
questions.explanation: The handbook places this on the driver: it is the responsibility of the driver to ensure that all passengers are buckled into their safety belts. It is not divided among the passengers.

questions.question: Which statement about safety belt responsibility is NOT correct?
choices: Each passenger is individually responsible for their own belt
The driver must ensure all passengers are buckled
Everyone in a passenger vehicle must wear a federally approved belt
A medical exception may require proof from the driver
questions.explanation: Responsibility is not left to each passenger — the handbook assigns it to the driver. The other three statements are exactly as the handbook puts them, including that proof of a medical condition may be required of the driver.

questions.question: What is the only legal exception to West Virginia's safety belt requirement?
choices: A person 18 years or older riding in the back seat
Any passenger riding in the back seat
Any adult who objects to wearing one
Drivers travelling under 25 mph
questions.explanation: The handbook describes exactly one legal exception: persons 18 years or older who are riding in the back seat. Age and seating position both have to be satisfied — a 16-year-old in the back is still required to buckle.

questions.question: A 16-year-old sits in the back seat of your car unbuckled. Is that allowed?
choices: No — the back-seat exception applies only to persons 18 or older
Yes — the exception covers anyone in the back seat
Yes — belts are required only in the front
Only if the trip is under a mile
questions.explanation: The exception is limited to persons 18 years or older riding in the back seat, so a 16-year-old must be belted wherever they sit. As driver, you are the one responsible for ensuring it.

About 10 percent
About 90 percent

questions.explanation: The handbook cites 45 to 50 percent. It explains the mechanism too: a belt spreads crash forces over the strongest parts of the body and helps occupants ride down a crash rather than being thrown forward or out of the vehicle.

questions.question: How does a safety belt protect an occupant, according to the handbook?
choices: It spreads crash forces over the strongest parts of the body
It absorbs the entire force of the impact
It works only in collisions below 30 mph
It protects the upper body but not the hips
questions.explanation: The handbook says a safety belt spreads crash forces over the strongest parts of the body and helps occupants ride down a crash. Used properly it also keeps you from being thrown forward or out of the vehicle, and keeps you in position on rough roads.

questions.question: Where should the lap belt sit?
choices: Snugly over the lower part of the hips
Across the soft part of the stomach
Loosely across the thighs
Above the waist, under the ribs
questions.explanation: The handbook says the lap belt should fit snugly and comfortably over the lower part of the hips, which still allows normal bending of the body. The hips are bone; the stomach is not, which is why a belt worn high can cause injury.

questions.question: A passenger tucks the shoulder belt behind their back and wears only the lap belt. Why is that a problem?
choices: Shoulder belts should be worn with lap belts for restraint and protection of the upper body
It is fine as long as the lap belt is snug
It only matters at speeds above 55 mph
Shoulder belts are optional for rear passengers
questions.explanation: The handbook says shoulder belts, which fit across the shoulder, should be worn with the lap belts for additional restraint and protection of the upper body. Tucking it away leaves the head and chest unrestrained.

questions.question: Under what age must a child be secured in a child passenger safety device in West Virginia?
choices: Under 8 years old
Under 4 years old
Under 12 years old
Under 6 years old
questions.explanation: West Virginia law requires a driver transporting a child under the age of 8 in a passenger automobile, van or pickup truck to secure the child in a child passenger safety device meeting applicable federal motor vehicle safety standards.

questions.question: A 7-year-old is 4 feet 10 inches tall. What does West Virginia law allow?
choices: A safety belt is sufficient, because the child is at least 4 feet 9 inches tall
A child safety seat is still required until age 8 regardless of height
The child may ride unrestrained in the back seat
A booster seat is required until age 12
questions.explanation: The law provides that if a child is under 8 but at least 4 feet 9 inches tall, a safety belt is sufficient. Height is the trigger because a belt only fits correctly, across the hips and shoulder, once the child is tall enough.

questions.question: Which factor lets a child under 8 use an ordinary safety belt instead of a child safety device?
choices: Being at least 4 feet 9 inches tall
Being at least 6 years old
Riding in the back seat
Travelling less than 5 miles
questions.explanation: Height, not age or seating position, is the deciding factor: the law states that if a child under 8 is at least 4 feet 9 inches tall, a safety belt is sufficient to meet the requirement.
